newsitem.title: USA: Ford, UAW negotiators seen finishing talks early.
newsitem.headline: Ford, UAW negotiators seen finishing talks early.

text.p: Negotiators for the United Auto Workers union and Ford Motor Co. were making significant progress Wednesday, industry sources said, heading toward what could be an unprecedented early settlement for a new national labor contract.
"My sense is they're close. An early settlement looks possible," said Harley Shaiken, a labor relations professor at the University of California at Berkeley.
Ford officials said meetings stretched into the evening Wednesday, but would not comment on when an agreement might be announced.
"I don't see anything to suggest that there will be an announcement tomorrow," said Ford spokesman Al Chambers. "The work is going along apace."
Ford Chief Financial Officer John Devine said Tuesday the two sides were making progress and were expected to reach an agreement by the contract's expiration Sept. 14.

Settling days early would not only be highly unusual, but could carry some risk for UAW President Stephen Yokich among the 104,000 UAW members who work at Ford. Union negotiators historically have taken contract talks down to the wire so as not to give the impression that they succumbed to company pressure.
Yokich, however, has demonstrated a willingness to throw out decades of tradition in the current round of talks, his first as president of the union.
"I suspect he's thinking what matters is the substance of what is produced, not the style," said Shaiken.

Ford, the No. 2 U.S. automaker, has reportedly voiced a willingness to address some of the union's job security concerns. That could include encouraging suppliers to allow union organizing efforts and possibly agreeing to a limit on the use of outside suppliers.
Such proposals could be a major disadvantage for General Motors Corp., which is trying to slash its costs by shifting more of its parts work to outside suppliers.

UAW officials rejected as "awful" and "dreadful" the comprehensive contract offer that GM made Tuesday. They said the offer didn't go far enough to guarantee employment levels, a crucial issue for the UAW as it seeks to keep its membership rolls high.
GM's action Tuesday was seen as an attempt by the automaker to present its offer to the union before it wraps things up at Ford and moves on to Chrysler Corp.

Meanwhile, Chrysler's top manufacturing executive arrived in Canada Wednesday to help iron out differences with tough-talking Canadian autoworkers. Chrysler plans to make its first economic proposal to the Canadian Auto Workers (CAW) union on Thursday, according to CAW President Buzz Hargrove.
"I'm certainly comfortable that they have the decision-makers here and the issue now will be whether we can find the resolve," Hargrove said.
On Tuesday, the CAW said it rejected an offer from Chrysler's Canadian unit that the two sides agree to a contract longer than the traditional three years.

Hargrove has been particularly vocal about his disappointment with Chrysler not being willing to limit its outsourcing. The union views outsourcing -- the practice of farming out work to outside suppliers -- as a threat to job security.
Hargrove has also said the union is willing to strike Chrysler if a deal is not reached by the Sept. 17 deadline.
